routes.description: Establish that naturally developed, reasons-responsive self-control constitutes the freedom relevant to moral agency and can support ordinary desert, responsibility, sanctions, and reactive practices without requiring ultimate self-creation or indeterminism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects practical control and moral competence to meaningful alternatives, distinguishes ordinary causation from responsibility-undermining interference, and explains why stable responsibility practices and proportionate consequences remain justified under determinism.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control is sufficient to justify compatibilist freedom, ordinary desert, and responsibility practices.

centralBridges.description: Define the relevant freedom through informed, unimpaired, reasons-responsive self-control rather than randomness or ultimate metaphysical authorship.
Explain how learning, reflection, practice, and moral education make agents sufficiently autonomous and accountable despite deterministic causal histories.
Justify proportionate, public, rule-governed sanctions and blame as components of a secure cooperative social order.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish deliberate interpersonal control from impersonal causal determination in assessing whether an agent's control has been displaced.
Account for morally condemnatory reactions as fitting and behavior-guiding responses to serious wrongdoing by competent adults.

routes.description: Establish that reasons-responsive agency does not supply the ultimate control required for basic desert, while showing that protection, deterrence, rehabilitation, moral engagement, and rule enforcement remain available on forward-looking grounds.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it separates practical agency from basic-desert responsibility, shows why neither determinism nor indeterminism supplies ultimate control, and provides non-desert foundations for justified social responses without retaining retribution or desert-dependent anger.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control does not justify basic desert and that defensible responsibility practices need not presuppose it.

centralBridges.description: Argue that agents are not ultimate sources of their characters and actions under either deterministic or indeterministic causal conditions.
Show that reasons-responsiveness and compatibilist agent control can matter practically without establishing desert-based blame or punishment.
Ground coercion, deterrence, rehabilitation, and rule enforcement in public safety, future risk, proportionality, and least-restrictive means.
Require an independent role for backward-looking desert beyond what consequentialist institutions and causal responsibility already provide.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use manipulation and malfunction cases to test whether internal psychological responsiveness is sufficient for responsibility.
Explain how evolved reactive attitudes and responsibility practices can be revised without surrendering their protective or communicative functions.

sections.title: Reasons-Responsive Control and the Ability to Do Otherwise
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether informed, unimpaired responsiveness to reasons constitutes the relevant practical control and meaningful alternative possibilities, or whether those capacities fall short of the freedom needed for desert.

sections.title: Sourcehood, Determinism, and Manipulation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deterministic histories undermine accountable agency, whether developed self-control supplies adequate sourcehood, and whether manipulation cases reveal a relevant gap between causation and control.

sections.title: Basic Desert and Ordinary Compatibilist Desert
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the central conceptual dispute over whether basic desert is required, whether ordinary conduct-sensitive desert is independently defensible, and whether reasons-responsive agency can bridge the two notions.

sections.title: Punishment, Public Safety, and Institutional Justification
sections.rationale: This issue compares rule-governed punishment and proportional sanctions with quarantine, deterrence, rehabilitation, and least-restrictive protection as foundations for legitimate coercive practices.

sections.title: Reactive Attitudes and Reform of Responsibility Practices
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether moral anger and condemnation are justified or indispensable, and whether evolved practices can instead be revised toward non-desert attitudes while retaining social regulation and moral communication.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Because responsibility practices are socially evolved and historically changeable, society can further reform them by relinquishing harmful notions of just desert and retribution.

sourceSpan.excerpt: um innocent people we we evolved from what are called honor cultures to individualistic cultures and part of that for me opens up the hope that we could evolve our moral responsibility practices further in a way that um relinquishes what i think of as outdated and unjustified and in my mind potentially harmful types of concepts like dessert and just desserts and retribution

moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs within Caruso's clearly marked response turn and presents his characteristic reformist argument against basic-desert practices.

components.text: Whether familiar and socially embedded desert practices are fixed or normatively indispensable
Whether evolved legal and responsibility practices can be further revised

response.rationale: The reply uses prior cultural change to argue that present desert and retributive practices are revisable rather than indispensable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is framed as hope for further reform and identifies the specific concepts proposed for relinquishment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest possibility claim is proportionate to the historical observation that responsibility cultures have changed.

charity.alternative: Evolved desert practices may be revisable yet retain valuable functions that replacement practices cannot duplicate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical change establishes possibility of reform, not the dispensability or harmfulness of every desert concept.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (84 and 82); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The honor-culture comparison supplies a concrete example, but harm and replacement-effectiveness claims remain lightly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary reform bridge by establishing that reactive and responsibility practices can change.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso invokes the historical movement from honor cultures to individualistic cultures as evidence that responsibility practices can evolve.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: If backward-looking desert performs genuine justificatory work in a punishment theory, that theory is mixed rather than purely consequentialist; if desert performs none, it should be removed.

moves.attributionBasis: Caruso resumes the conceptual challenge in an extended turn, contrasting his forward-looking conversational model with Dennett's retained backward-looking element.

components.text: Whether consequentialist desert performs independent justificatory work in punishment

response.rationale: The reply identifies a dilemma: justificatory desert makes the theory mixed, while nonjustificatory desert is dispensable, undermining the claimed purely consequentialist position.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two exhaustive roles considered for desert are clearly stated and tied to distinct classificatory consequences.

charity.alternative: Desert may be a rule-internal concept generated and justified by consequentialist institutional design.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The opponent's expressed consequentialist desert supplies the relevant premise, though comparison with sophisticated rule-consequentialist accounts is compressed.

representationalCharity.rationale: The dilemma accommodates instrumental desert language while precisely challenging any claimed independent backward-looking role.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Consequentialist reasons can justify a rule-governed punishment system even though individual adjudication properly applies agreed rules rather than recalculating the consequences of punishment in each case.

components.text: Whether rule-governed punishment can remain consequentialist when adjudicators apply rules nonconsequentially

Whether stable rules can govern differentiated legal judgments

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes consequentialist system justification from rule-bound adjudication and explains why case-by-case recalculation would undermine law.

precisionFindings.rationale: System-level justification and case-level rule application are distinctly stated, with their respective scopes made explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Rule stability supports limits on case recalculation, but categorical exclusion of consequences may overlook exceptional-case safeguards.

charity.alternative: A rule-consequentialist system can explain punishment rules without retaining backward-looking desert terminology.
charity.decisiveQualification: The system-versus-act distinction answers the mixed-theory charge but not the separate dispensability challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rule-versus-act distinction coherently reconciles consequentialist design with noncalculative adjudication, with desert still underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The game and referee analogy concretely illustrates rule application, though the empirical claim about legal respect lacks verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central institutions bridge through a rule-governed consequentialist account of punishment.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett uses rule-following and referee analogies to distinguish system justification from consequence calculation in individual cases.

moves.proposition: Desert-dependent moral anger can be replaced by attitudes such as disappointment or sorrow while retaining, and potentially improving, the practical work of interpersonal responsibility practices.
